title: The Medicine King (Kern ch. 22)
hookLine: a story of total devotion from a past life; the tradition reads it as an image of offering, never an instruction

lines: AN OFFERING THAT HOLDS NOTHING BACK.
cards: This is a hard story, and it's told here the way this path reads it: as an image, not an instruction.
Chapter twenty-two in Kern's numbering goes back to a past life of the bodhisattva called the Medicine King, the one who offered the first spell yesterday.
Then he had another name, Sarvasattvapriyadarshana, roughly, the one all beings are glad to see. He had heard this teaching from his Buddha, and he wanted to give an offering that held nothing back.

teach.h: AN OFFERING WITH NOTHING HELD BACK.
teach.b: First, the story. This bodhisattva first offers flowers and incense to his Buddha, then decides that no outward gift is enough.
He offers his own body as a lamp, and the light, the sutra says, shines across countless worlds, and the Buddhas there praise the offering.

In a later life he offers his arms at the stupas, and by a vow of truth they are restored. It is told in the sutra's large, dreamlike way, with worlds and ages beyond counting. Second, how it is heard here.
Buddhist teachers who comment on this chapter have read it in different ways.

teach.h: HEARD AS AN IMAGE, NEVER A TASK.
teach.b: On this path it is heard as a picture of devotion pushed to its edge, and never as something to do. Nobody here is asked to harm their body. Buddhist precepts begin with not taking life.
If this story stirs something heavy for you, please reach out today to someone you trust, or to a local crisis line. In the US, call or text 988, any hour. Third, the medicine.

teach.h: A LAMP, A BOAT, A DOCTOR.
teach.b: The chapter then praises the sutra itself, and the images are gentle: like fire for someone who is cold, clothing for someone who has none, a boat for someone crossing water, a lamp in the dark, a doctor for the sick.
That last one fits the name. The Medicine King is a healer, and the teaching he loves is medicine.
Fourth, what remains for an ordinary day. Strip away the vast scale, and the chapter asks a simple question. What would it mean to give something your whole self, not just the leftovers?
Most days the answer is small: your full attention, given without holding part of it back.

how: In East Asian Buddhism, the Medicine King chapter is recited and studied as a teaching on devotion and on the sutra as medicine; offerings of light, such as lamps and candles set before Buddha images, are part of Buddhist devotion.

o: a healer bodhisattva, a picture of total devotion
a doctor who cured the Buddha of a long fever
a king who built the first hospitals for monks

games.q: you love a teaching and want to honor it with nothing held back. on an ordinary day, what does this path take from the Medicine King's story?
o: give your full attention, not the leftovers
decide devotion is only for saints
games.why: the story is heard as an image of devotion, never an instruction; on an ordinary day it points to giving your whole attention.

practice: For these two minutes, give your whole attention to one thing, the breath coming in and going out: not half of it while the other half plans dinner, all of it, as an offering.
When attention wanders, and it will, bring it back the way you'd set a gift down carefully, not the way you'd correct a mistake. Each return is the offering made again.

wordCard.voice: The Medicine King. Bhaishajyaraja, the healer bodhisattva of the Lotus Sutra, whose past life is told as an image of devotion with nothing held back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: an offering of devotion. Given whole, not as leftovers. Rest well.
